Question: An ice cube on a lab bench at 10 °C melts; an identical cube in a freezer at −10 °C stays solid. Melting spreads the water molecules into more arrangements either way, and a thermometer in the surrounding air shows heat flowing into the ice. What decides whether the ice melts: the entropy change of the ice, of its surroundings, or both?
Answer: ΔS(sys) = +22.1 J/K (melting increases dispersal). ΔS(surr) = −q ÷ T = −6000 J ÷ T: −21.2 J/K at 283.15 K, −22.8 J/K at 263.15 K. ΔS(univ) = ΔS(sys) + ΔS(surr): +0.9 J/K at 10 °C (spontaneous), −0.7 J/K at −10 °C (not). Second law: spontaneous if and only if ΔS(univ) > 0. The same heat costs colder surroundings more entropy. (OpenStax Example 16.4.)
Target concept: A process is spontaneous when ΔS(univ) = ΔS(sys) + ΔS(surr) > 0; the surroundings' term, −ΔH ÷ T, depends on temperature.

Question: Squeeze an instant cold pack and the ammonium nitrate inside dissolves in water; a thermometer on the pack drops toward 0 °C. The dissolving draws heat from your hand, yet it runs on its own. How can an endothermic process be spontaneous?
Answer: NH₄NO₃(s) → NH₄⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq): ΔH° = +28.1 kJ (endothermic); ΔS°(sys) = +108.7 J/K (ions dispersed from a lattice into solution). ΔS(surr) = −ΔH ÷ T = −94.2 J/K at 298 K. ΔS(univ) = +14.6 J/K > 0: spontaneous. The entropy gained by dispersing the ions outweighs the entropy the surroundings lose.
Target concept: An endothermic process is spontaneous when the system's entropy gain outweighs the surroundings' loss: ΔS(univ) > 0.

Question: On a humid day, water vapor condenses into droplets on a glass of ice water. Condensing gathers the molecules into a liquid, so the water's entropy falls, yet the dew forms on its own, and a thermometer taped to the glass shows it warming slightly as the droplets form. Where does the entropy go?
Answer: H₂O(g) → H₂O(l): ΔS(sys) = −118.8 J/K; ΔH = −44.01 kJ released to the surroundings; ΔS(surr) = +44,010 J ÷ 298 K = +147.7 J/K; ΔS(univ) = +28.9 J/K > 0: spontaneous. At 400 K, ΔS(surr) is only +110 J/K and ΔS(univ) < 0: no condensation.
Target concept: An exothermic process can lower the system's entropy and still be spontaneous, because the heat released raises the surroundings' entropy more.

Question: An iron nail left outdoors rusts: four iron atoms and three molecules of oxygen gas become two units of solid iron(III) oxide. The system loses a huge amount of entropy, yet rusting happens on its own. Which part of the universe gains the entropy?
Answer: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃: ΔS°(sys) = −550.0 J/K (three moles of gas consumed). ΔH° = −1648.4 kJ released; ΔS(surr) = +1,648,400 J ÷ 298 K = +5531 J/K; ΔS(univ) = +4982 J/K. The heat released to the surroundings creates far more entropy than the system loses.
Target concept: For strongly exothermic reactions the surroundings' entropy gain dominates ΔS(univ).
